planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, fertile soil; this interspecific kabocha-butternut cross needs a long, vigorous vine run and rewards gardeners with unusually heavy yields even in stressed conditions.

directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills after all danger of frost has passed, spacing hills 6-8 feet apart to accommodate the exceptionally vigorous vines. Tetsukabuto is a hybrid cross between a kabocha-type Cucurbita maxima and a moschata parent, prized by growers for hybrid vigor that shrugs off vine borers and powdery mildew far better than either parent species alone. Fruits are near-round, 4-6 pounds, with dark, mottled black-green skin and deep orange-yellow flesh that is dry, dense, and nutty-sweet, closer in eating quality to a fine kabocha than a butternut. Cure in a warm spot for a week after harvest before moving to cool storage, where the fruit keeps remarkably well, often into the following spring.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; a semi-restricted vine that can be grown in-ground or trellised, producing single-serving butternuts ideal for small households and space-limited gardens.

directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after the last frost in fertile, well-drained soil; Butterbaby's semi-compact vines can be left to sprawl or trained up a trellis to save garden space. Butterbaby is a hybrid mini butternut bred for uniform, single-portion fruits weighing about a half to one and a half pounds, with the same tan skin and rich, nutty-sweet, deep orange flesh as full-size butternuts but scaled down for one or two servings. Plants set fruit heavily and consistently, making them well suited to succession harvests through the fall. Harvest when the rind has hardened and turned fully tan, cure for a week or two, and store in a cool, dry spot for several months.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, fertile soil; a rare 19th-century Australian heirloom valued for its unmistakable three-lobed shape and exceptionally long storage life.

directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in enriched, well-drained soil, giving the sprawling vines 6-8 feet of room. Triamble is an Australian heirloom dating to at least the 1820s, named for its distinctive tri-lobed, clover-like shape formed by three fused lobes curving back toward the stem; the tough, slate-blue-grey rind gave rise to its nickname 'Ironbark pumpkin.' Fruits average around 8 pounds and hold sweet, dry, deep-orange flesh similar in quality to Queensland Blue. The hard rind makes Triamble notably difficult to cut but also gives it outstanding keeping quality, with properly cured fruit reported to store for a year or more in a cool, dry space.

common_name: First Prize Pumpkin (F1 Giant Pumpkin Hybrid)

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant after last frost in deeply enriched soil; a hybrid giant-pumpkin selection bred for competitive weigh-off growers wanting reliably massive fruit without decades of seed-line selection.

directions: Start indoors 2-3 weeks before last frost or direct sow into hills of heavily composted soil, allowing at least 15-20 feet of space per plant since a single vine can spread over several hundred square feet. First Prize is a hybrid giant pumpkin bred for competitive growers, capable of producing fruit up to 300 pounds under intensive management, though most home-garden fruit lands well under that with less aggressive pruning and feeding. For maximum size, growers typically remove all but one or two developing fruits per vine and pinch side shoots to direct the plant's energy into the remaining pumpkins. Heavy, consistent watering and monthly feeding through the growing season are essential; harvest before hard frost once the rind hardens and the stem begins to dry.
sources: University of New Hampshire Cooperative Extension

common_name: Porcelain Doll Pumpkin (F1 Pink Cinderella-Type Pumpkin)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in rich, well-amended soil; a hybrid Cinderella-type pumpkin whose flattened fruit deepens from pale cream to soft peachy pink as it matures, prized for both display and eating quality.

directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in fertile, well-drained soil, spacing hills 6-8 feet apart to give the vigorous vines room to spread. Porcelain Doll is a hybrid Cinderella-type pumpkin producing flattened, deeply ribbed fruit in the 20-24 pound range that shifts from pale yellow to cream and finally to a distinctive soft pink as it fully ripens on the vine. Beneath the showy pink rind lies a thick wall of sweet, dense, edible flesh that holds up well for roasting and pureeing, making this variety popular with both farmstand growers and cooks. Harvest once the rind has fully hardened and colored, then cure for one to two weeks before moving to cool, dry storage.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; a 1999 All-America Selections winner with true bush habit and short vines, making it one of the most space-efficient pumpkins for containers or small beds.

directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in warm, fertile soil; Wee-B-Little's compact bush habit and short 6-8 foot vines mean it needs far less garden space than standard pumpkins and grows well in large containers. This 1999 All-America Selections winner produces three to four miniature, deep-orange pumpkins per plant, each weighing only 8 ounces to a pound, with smooth skin that takes paint and carving detail beautifully. The uniform bush habit and heavy fruit set make it a favorite for classroom gardens and children's plots where kids can grow and claim their own small pumpkin. Harvest once the rind hardens and resists a fingernail scratch, leaving 3-4 inches of stem attached to extend shelf life.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, fertile soil; a reliable hybrid jack-o'-lantern type valued by growers for uniform, well-shaped fruit and strong handles suited to market sales.

directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in warm, well-drained soil, spacing hills 6 feet apart for the vigorous vines. Magic Lantern is a hybrid carving pumpkin producing classically shaped, medium-ribbed fruit in the 16-24 pound range with bright orange skin and a sturdy, well-attached handle that holds up through harvest and transport to market. Its uniform round-to-slightly-tall shape and consistent sizing make it a dependable choice for growers selling by the piece at pumpkin patches and farm stands. Harvest when the rind has fully colored and hardened, before the first hard frost, and cure briefly in a warm, dry spot to toughen the skin for longer display life.

common_name: Warty Goblin Pumpkin (F1 Warted Novelty Pumpkin)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, fertile soil; a novelty hybrid grown for its heavily warted rind rather than eating quality, popular for spooky fall displays.

directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in fertile, well-drained soil, giving vines 6 feet of room to sprawl. Warty Goblin is a novelty hybrid pumpkin bred purely for eerie ornamental appeal, producing 8-20 pound fruit with a hard orange rind studded in dense, gnarled green warts that persist for weeks after harvest before slowly fading. The plants show useful intermediate resistance to powdery mildew, helping the vines stay productive later into the season than many older open-pollinated types. Because the flesh is stringy and thin compared to culinary pumpkins, Warty Goblin is grown strictly for Halloween decorating rather than cooking; harvest once the rind has fully hardened and cure briefly before display.

common_name: Knuckle Head Pumpkin (F1 Warted Novelty Pumpkin)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, fertile soil; part of the Superfreak series of warted novelty pumpkins bred by Siegers Seed Co. for exaggerated, gnarled rind texture.

directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in warm, well-drained soil, spacing hills 6 feet apart for the sprawling vines. Knuckle Head is a hybrid novelty pumpkin from the Superfreak series, producing 12-16 pound, slightly tall, dark-orange fruit densely covered in gnarled warts that range from dark green through light green to orange; unlike some warty types, wart color is not a reliable ripeness indicator here. The variety carries useful powdery mildew resistance, which helps keep foliage productive through the fruit-finishing stage of the season. Grown almost exclusively for its shock-value texture at pumpkin patches and fall markets rather than for eating, it should be harvested once the rind is fully hard and stored in a cool, dry spot for display.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in deeply enriched soil; a giant white pumpkin that needs a long, warm season and heavy feeding to reach its full 60-90 pound potential.

directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in heavily composted soil, spacing hills at least 8-10 feet apart to accommodate the large-fruited vines. Full Moon is a giant white pumpkin producing smooth, lightly sutured fruit that commonly reaches 60-90 pounds and stands roughly 3 feet tall by 2 feet wide under good growing conditions, with a long 120-day-plus season needed to size up fully. The pale rind is retained best when fruit is left to mature fully on the vine rather than harvested early, and consistent deep watering through fruit set is important to avoid rind cracking on such large specimens. Harvest before hard frost once the rind has hardened completely, and handle carefully since the size and weight make the fruit prone to bruising and stem breakage.
